\title{Correctness-Gated Reinforcement Learning for\\
High-Frequency DSP Accelerator RTL, Validated on Silicon}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Mohamed Amine Hallam}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen} \\

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Large language models can emit syntactically valid Verilog, but functional
correctness alone is not a useful engineering target: a register-transfer level
(RTL) description is valuable only if it is both correct and fast enough to
close timing on the target device. Existing work optimises these objectives
separately, evaluates them with synthesis estimates rather than measurement, and
rarely separates generalisation to unseen parameters from memorisation of the
training grid. We propose a correctness-gated reinforcement learning method in
which the reward of a generated design is its predicted maximum operating
frequency \emph{if and only if} an input/output-equivalence oracle certifies the
design correct, and zero otherwise. Applied to five families of streaming DSP
accelerators spanning three circuit classes, and evaluated under a held-out
split frozen before training, the method raises mean WNS-derived Vivado
\fmax{} on thirty unseen designs from $86.5$ to $\best{211.3}$~MHz under
parameter interpolation ($+144\%$) and from $78.5$ to $\best{174.2}$~MHz under
extrapolation ($+122\%$), exceeding a perfect-selector best-of-eight baseline in
both regimes. The recipe transfers unmodified to a second base model, and both
models converge to the same measured frequency ceiling. Five held-out design
pairs placed on a Zynq-7020 and swept in hardware sustain $2.25$--$3.40\times$
the measured clock of the supervised baseline with zero spread across repeated
runs. We further document a caught case of reward hacking in which the learned
surrogate reported $188.6$~MHz for designs measuring $36$--$40$~MHz, quantify
how far the surrogate's discrimination degrades once structurally dissimilar
circuit classes are added, and report the families where the method yields no
frequency gain together with the mechanism that explains it.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
RTL generation, reinforcement learning, large language models, FPGA,
design space exploration, reward hacking
\end{IEEEkeywords}
